html:
Bubonic plague reached Bombay in September 1896, and over the next decades it spread across India and killed some ten million people. It was part of the third plague pandemic, which began in southwest China and reached Hong Kong in 1894.

The disease is carried by fleas on rats, and it spread from the port along the railways. The British answered with harsh measures under a new Epidemic Diseases Act of 1897: soldiers searched homes, the sick were taken to camps, houses were burned and travellers checked. Many Indians saw this as an assault on their homes and customs.

In Pune the anger turned violent. In 1897 the Chapekar brothers shot the plague commissioner, W. C. Rand. The nationalist Bal Gangadhar Tilak, who had attacked the measures in print, was jailed for sedition.

Science moved too. In Bombay in 1897 Waldemar Haffkine made a plague vaccine and tested it on himself; his laboratory became the Haffkine Institute. Plague lingered in India into the 1920s and later, the worst outbreak since the Black Death.
